CRIMINAL WAGE THEFT AS GRAND THEFT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for John Smith · Acme Corp.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California Penal Code section 487m -- the state's criminal statute allowing intentional theft of wages to be punished as grand theft -- along with Labor Code section 1197.1's separate, pre-existing civil penalty scheme for underpayment of the minimum wage. It is prepared by Jane Doe concerning a situation described here as: unpaid final wages and tips, involving Acme Corp. and John Smith, in an amount currently identified as approximately $2,500.

Penal Code section 487m is a criminal statute. A violation of it is prosecuted, if at all, by a public prosecutor -- a district attorney or the Attorney General -- not through a private lawsuit. This information sheet does not initiate, threaten, or request any criminal investigation or prosecution, and it does not state that any specific conduct described above does or does not violate section 487m; that is a case-specific determination this document does not make.

This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter and Wage Claim with the California Labor Commissioner (Berman Hearing) -- Information Sheet documents, both of which describe civil remedies for unpaid wages rather than this separate criminal statute.

THE DOLLAR THRESHOLDS THAT MAKE INTENTIONAL WAGE THEFT PUNISHABLE AS GRAND THEFT
Penal Code section 487m, added to California law in 2021 by Assembly Bill 1003 and effective January 1, 2022, states that the intentional theft of wages may be punished as grand theft once it crosses one of two dollar thresholds measured over any consecutive 12-month period: an amount greater than $950 taken from any one employee, or an amount totaling $2,350 or more in the aggregate taken from two or more employees. The statute's own text uses the word "may," not "shall" or "must" -- classification as grand theft under this section is something a prosecution may pursue once a threshold is crossed, not an automatic legal consequence that attaches the moment a threshold is crossed. The statute's threshold is expressly stated to apply "notwithstanding" two other Labor Code sections, 215 and 216, meaning it operates independently of whatever those two sections separately provide.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Notwithstanding Sections 215 and 216 of the Labor Code, the intentional theft of wages in an amount greater than nine hundred fifty dollars ($950) from any one employee, or two thousand three hundred fifty dollars ($2,350) in the aggregate from two or more employees, by an employer in any consecutive 12-month period may be punished as grand theft."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 487m(a) (California Legislative Information text), California's criminal wage-theft grand-theft statute, dollar thresholds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=487m.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Penal Code § 487m(a)), used as real evidence of the dollar thresholds and their permissive "may be punished" phrasing -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific situation, and not a claim that any specific amount of unpaid compensation has or has not crossed either threshold. This clause quotes a single subdivision, § 487m(a); the statute's remaining subdivisions -- its definition of "theft of wages," its expanded definitions of "employee" and "employer," its restitution and civil-action-preservation provisions, and its relationship to the general grand theft statute -- are addressed in this document's companion clauses, not repeated here. Labor Code sections 215 and 216, which this subdivision references by name as sections it operates "notwithstanding," were not independently fetched or verified for this document; this clause reports only that § 487m(a) itself references them, not what they themselves say. This document does not independently verify, through Penal Code section 487 itself or through case law, what dollar threshold applies to grand theft generally outside this specific wage-theft context, or how a sentencing court would actually apply this section's "may be punished" language in a specific case; a CourtListener case-law search for judicial decisions interpreting § 487m, attempted for this document, returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be reviewed, so that gap is disclosed here rather than filled with an unverified assertion. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific employer's conduct did or did not cross either threshold, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

WHAT COUNTS AS "THEFT OF WAGES": THE DEFINITION AND ITS INTENT ELEMENT
Penal Code section 487m defines "theft of wages," for purposes of this statute, as the intentional deprivation of wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation, by unlawful means, done with the knowledge that the wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation is due to the employee under the law. The statute borrows its definitions of two of these four categories from elsewhere in the Labor Code rather than defining them itself: "wages" takes the definition already stated in Labor Code section 200, and "gratuities" takes the definition already stated in Labor Code section 350. Labor Code section 200 defines "wages" broadly, as all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whatever method -- time, task, piece, commission, or otherwise -- is used to fix or ascertain the amount. Labor Code section 350 defines "gratuity" to include any tip, gratuity, money, or part of one that a patron of a business has paid, given, or left for an employee over and above the amount actually due the business for the services, goods, food, drink, or articles the patron received. Section 487m's own text does not separately define "benefits" or "other compensation" beyond these words' ordinary meaning; the statute leaves both categories otherwise undefined.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) For purposes of this section, “theft of wages” is the intentional deprivation of wages, as defined in Section 200 of the Labor Code, gratuities, as defined in Section 350 of the Labor Code, benefits, or other compensation, by unlawful means, with the knowledge that the wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation is due to the employee under the law."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 487m(b) (California Legislative Information text), California's criminal wage-theft grand-theft statute, definition of "theft of wages" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=487m.)
  "(a) “Wages” includes all amounts for labor performed by employees of every description, whether the amount is fixed or ascertained by the standard of time, task, piece, commission basis, or other method of calculation."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 200(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "wages" (cross-referenced by Penal Code § 487m(b)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=200.)
  "(e) “Gratuity” includes any tip, gratuity, money, or part thereof that has been paid or given to or left for an employee by a patron of a business over and above the actual amount due the business for services rendered or for goods, food, drink, or articles sold or served to the patron. Any amounts paid directly by a patron to a dancer employed by an employer subject to Industrial Welfare Commission Order No. 5 or 10 shall be deemed a gratuity."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 350(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, definition of "gratuity" (cross-referenced by Penal Code § 487m(b)) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=350.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text -- one subdivision of Cal. Penal Code § 487m (subdivision (b)) together with two Labor Code sections it incorporates by cross-reference, Cal. Lab. Code § 200(a) and § 350(e) -- used as real evidence of what "theft of wages" means for this statute's purposes, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific situation, and not a claim that any specific conduct did or did not meet this definition. The two Labor Code citations are cross-referenced definitions section 487m itself borrows by name, not independent corroborating sources for the same proposition; they are quoted here because section 487m's own text does not restate them. Labor Code § 200 contains a second subdivision, (b), defining "labor" -- not quoted here because section 487m does not cross-reference it. Labor Code § 350 contains five other subdivisions, (a) through (d) and (f), defining "employer," "employee," "employing," "agent," and "business" for its own article -- not quoted here for the same reason; only its gratuity definition, subdivision (e), is what section 487m actually cross-references. This clause does not address what case law, if any, has said about the meaning of "intentional," "unlawful means," or the knowledge requirement in subdivision (b), or about the undefined terms "benefits" and "other compensation"; a CourtListener case-law search attempted for this document returned a daily rate-limit error before any results could be reviewed, and given that this statute took effect January 1, 2022, this document does not independently know whether published case law interpreting it yet exists. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific deprivation of wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation was intentional, was accomplished by unlawful means, or was done with the knowledge this statute requires.

SECTION 487M'S EXPANDED DEFINITIONS OF "EMPLOYEE" AND "EMPLOYER"
For purposes of Penal Code section 487m specifically, the statute expands who counts as an "employee" and an "employer" beyond the conventional employment relationship: "employee" includes an independent contractor, and "employer" includes the hiring entity of an independent contractor. This means a hiring entity's intentional, unlawful-means deprivation of compensation due to an independent contractor -- not only a common-law or statutory employee -- can fall within this statute's reach, once the statute's other elements (the dollar thresholds and the intent element, addressed in this document's companion clauses) are also met.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) For purposes of this section, “employee” includes an independent contractor and “employer” includes the hiring entity of an independent contractor."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 487m(c) (California Legislative Information text), California's criminal wage-theft grand-theft statute, expanded "employee"/"employer" definitions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=487m.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, a single subdivision of the same section addressed throughout this document -- Cal. Penal Code § 487m(c) -- used as real evidence of who this specific statute treats as an "employee" and "employer," not a claim about which state's law governs any specific working relationship, and not a claim that any specific person is or is not an independent contractor under California law generally. Section 487m's own text does not itself define "independent contractor" or "hiring entity"; this document does not independently trace those terms to California's separate statutory and case-law tests for distinguishing an independent contractor from an employee (for example, the ABC test codified elsewhere in the Labor Code), and does not determine that any specific working relationship is or is not an independent-contractor relationship. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific person is a covered "employee" or "employer" under this section, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

RESTITUTION, THE PRESERVED CIVIL ACTION, AND THE RELATIONSHIP TO THE GENERAL GRAND THEFT STATUTE
Penal Code section 487m addresses what happens to the underlying compensation once a prosecution under this section occurs, and how this criminal statute relates to two other legal avenues. First, wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation that are the subject of a section 487m prosecution may be recovered as restitution, through the general criminal restitution procedures set out in Penal Code sections 1202.4 and 1203.1. Second, the statute expressly states that it does not prohibit the employee, or the Labor Commissioner, from separately commencing a civil action to seek the remedies the Labor Code otherwise provides for the same underlying acts -- meaning a criminal prosecution under section 487m and a civil wage claim or lawsuit over the same conduct are not mutually exclusive under this statute's own terms. Third, section 487m states that it does not itself change, expand, or limit the scope of conduct already prohibited by California's general grand theft statute, Penal Code section 487; section 487m adds a specific, wage-focused path to a grand theft charge without altering what section 487 itself separately prohibits.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(d) Wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation that are the subject of a prosecution under this section may be recovered as restitution in accordance with Sections 1202.4 and 1203.1. This section does not prohibit the employee or the Labor Commissioner from commencing a civil action to seek remedies provided for under the Labor Code for acts prosecuted under this section."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 487m(d) (California Legislative Information text), California's criminal wage-theft grand-theft statute, restitution and preserved civil action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=487m.)
  "(e) This section does not constitute a change in, and does not expand or limit the scope of conduct prohibited by, Section 487."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 487m(e) (California Legislative Information text), California's criminal wage-theft grand-theft statute, relationship to the general grand theft statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=487m.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, two subdivisions of the same section addressed throughout this document -- Cal. Penal Code § 487m(d) and (e) -- used as real evidence of the restitution mechanism, the preserved civil action, and the no-change-to-section-487 language, not a claim about which state's law governs any specific matter, and not a claim that restitution would be ordered, or that a civil action would succeed, in any specific case. This document does not independently fetch or verify the text of Penal Code sections 1202.4 or 1203.1 (the general criminal restitution provisions cross-referenced here), or the text of Penal Code section 487 itself (the general grand theft statute this section says it does not change); each is treated here as a named cross-reference within § 487m's own verified text, not as independently researched authority. This corpus's existing Final Wage Payment / Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter and Wage Claim with the California Labor Commissioner (Berman Hearing) -- Information Sheet documents describe what those separate civil remedies actually involve; this clause states only that section 487m itself preserves access to remedies of that kind, not what a specific civil claim arising from the same facts would recover. This clause is informational only: it does not itself seek restitution, does not commence or describe the mechanics of any specific civil action, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

A SEPARATE, PRE-EXISTING CIVIL TRACK: LABOR CODE SECTION 1197.1'S MINIMUM-WAGE CIVIL PENALTY
Separately from Penal Code section 487m's criminal grand-theft classification, California law has long provided its own, distinct civil penalty scheme for a related but narrower problem: paying an employee less than the applicable minimum wage. Labor Code section 1197.1 states that an employer or other person who pays or causes to be paid to an employee a wage less than the minimum fixed by an applicable state or local law, or by a wage order, is subject to a civil penalty, restitution of wages, liquidated damages payable to the employee, and any applicable waiting-time penalties -- enforced administratively by the Labor Commissioner through the citation, hearing, and appeal procedures that section and related sections set out, not through a criminal prosecution. Section 1197.1 was last amended effective January 1, 2021, before Assembly Bill 1003 added Penal Code section 487m in 2022; nothing in section 1197.1's own current text refers to section 487m, to grand theft, or to either of section 487m's dollar thresholds, and section 487m's text does not refer to section 1197.1 either. The two statutes address overlapping subject matter -- an employer's failure to pay compensation actually owed -- through separate legal tracks with separate triggers, separate enforcing bodies, and separate consequences: section 1197.1's civil penalty applies specifically to minimum-wage underpayment, without the dollar thresholds section 487m requires, while section 487m's criminal classification applies to the broader category of intentionally, unlawfully withheld wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation, but only once one of its own dollar thresholds is crossed.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any employer or other person acting either individually or as an officer, agent, or employee of another person, who pays or causes to be paid to any employee a wage less than the minimum fixed by an applicable state or local law, or by an order of the commission, shall be subject to a civil penalty, restitution of wages, liquidated damages payable to the employee, and any applicable penalties imposed pursuant to Section 203 as follows:"
  — Cal. Labor Code § 1197.1(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Labor Code, minimum-wage civil penalty (separate civil track from Penal Code § 487m) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1197.1.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1197.1(a)), used as real evidence of what California's civil minimum-wage penalty scheme says and how it differs in structure from Penal Code section 487m -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific employer's conduct would trigger one statute, the other, both, or neither. This clause quotes the same subdivision, § 1197.1(a), that this corpus's existing Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice to Employee -- Information Sheet document also quotes, in a different clause, for a different purpose (there, to show that § 1197.1 does not itself reference the separate hiring-notice statute, Labor Code § 2810.5); this document independently re-fetched and re-verified that same subdivision's text, twice, with two different User-Agent headers, rather than assuming the earlier quote remained current, and confirms it is unchanged. Section 1197.1 contains eleven further subdivisions, (b) through (l), addressing citation procedure, hearing and appeal rights, and other administrative mechanics; those are not restated here, since this corpus's existing DLSE Wage Claim and Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter documents already describe the administrative wage-claim process (Labor Code §§ 98 through 98.2) that operates alongside section 1197.1's citation authority in practice, and duplicating that description here was judged unnecessary. This document does not independently verify, through case law, how often conduct severe enough to cross section 487m's dollar thresholds also happens to involve minimum-wage underpayment within the meaning of section 1197.1, or vice versa; the two statutes' overlap or non-overlap in any specific case is a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific employer's conduct is or is not a minimum-wage violation under section 1197.1, is or is not conduct described by section 487m, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.

RECORD OF REVIEW AND SIGNATURE
I certify that the description above reflects my understanding of the situation as of the date below, and that I have reviewed the statutory information in this sheet.

Prepared by: Jane Doe
Executed on January 1, 2026 at Los Angeles, California.

Signature: _________________________

It is not a police report, a district attorney complaint, a DLSE wage claim, or a civil demand letter, and completing or signing it does not file anything with any prosecutor, court, or agency, does not initiate a criminal investigation or prosecution, does not determine that Acme Corp. owes John Smith any wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation, does not determine that any conduct described above is or is not a crime, does not constitute legal advice, and is not a substitute for consulting a licensed attorney or a public prosecutor's office.]

Labor Code section 1197.1 states that an employer or other person who pays or causes to be paid to an employee a wage less than the minimum fixed by an applicable state or local law, or by a wage order, is subject to a civil penalty, restitution of wages, liquidated damages payable to the employee, and any applicable waiting-time penalties -- enforced administratively by the Labor Commissioner through the citation, hearing, and appeal procedures that section and related sections set out, not through a criminal prosecution. Section 1197.1 was last amended effective January 1, 2021, before Assembly Bill 1003 added Penal Code section 487m in 2022; nothing in section 1197.1's own current text refers to section 487m, to grand theft, or to either of section 487m's dollar thresholds, and section 487m's text does not refer to section 1197.1 either. The two statutes address overlapping subject matter -- an employer's failure to pay compensation actually owed -- through separate legal tracks with separate triggers, separate enforcing bodies, and separate consequences: section 1197.1's civil penalty applies specifically to minimum-wage underpayment, without the dollar thresholds section 487m requires, while section 487m's criminal classification applies to the broader category of intentionally, unlawfully withheld wages, gratuities, benefits, or other compensation, but only once one of its own dollar thresholds is crossed.

expectedJSON.gap: This is one state's statute (Cal. Lab. Code § 1197.1(a)), used as real evidence of what California's civil minimum-wage penalty scheme says and how it differs in structure from Penal Code section 487m -- not a claim about which state's law governs any specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific employer's conduct would trigger one statute, the other, both, or neither. This clause quotes the same subdivision, § 1197.1(a), that this corpus's existing Wage Theft Prevention Act Notice to Employee -- Information Sheet document also quotes, in a different clause, for a different purpose (there, to show that § 1197.1 does not itself reference the separate hiring-notice statute, Labor Code § 2810.5); this document independently re-fetched and re-verified that same subdivision's text, twice, with two different User-Agent headers, rather than assuming the earlier quote remained current, and confirms it is unchanged. Section 1197.1 contains eleven further subdivisions, (b) through (l), addressing citation procedure, hearing and appeal rights, and other administrative mechanics; those are not restated here, since this corpus's existing DLSE Wage Claim and Waiting-Time Penalty Demand Letter documents already describe the administrative wage-claim process (Labor Code §§ 98 through 98.2) that operates alongside section 1197.1's citation authority in practice, and duplicating that description here was judged unnecessary. This document does not independently verify, through case law, how often conduct severe enough to cross section 487m's dollar thresholds also happens to involve minimum-wage underpayment within the meaning of section 1197.1, or vice versa; the two statutes' overlap or non-overlap in any specific case is a fact-specific question this clause does not resolve. This clause is informational only: it does not itself determine that any specific employer's conduct is or is not a minimum-wage violation under section 1197.1, is or is not conduct described by section 487m, and does not determine the outcome of any specific matter.
